topics.name: Living and Non-Living Things
topics.summary: How to tell what is alive from what has never been alive.

topics.name: Parts of a Plant
topics.summary: Roots, stem, leaves, flower — and what each one does.

objectives.text: List the things all living things do.
Sort things into living and non-living.
Explain why moving does not always mean alive.

keyTerms.definition: Something that grows, feeds, breathes, moves and produces young.
Something that has never been alive.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: It seems easy to say what is alive. But a river moves and is not alive, while a seed sits still and is. This lesson gives you a proper test instead of a guess.

sections.heading: What all living things do
sections.body:
Living things all do these:

    They GROW — they get bigger over time
    They FEED — they take in food
    They BREATHE — they take in air
    They MOVE — even plants turn towards light
    They MAKE YOUNG — they produce more of their own kind
    They RESPOND — they react to what is around them

A goat does all six. A tree does all six, just more slowly than you would notice by watching.

A stone does none.

sections.heading: Why "it moves" is not enough
sections.body:
This is the part people get wrong most often.

A river moves. A car moves. Smoke moves. None of them is alive.

Why not? Because moving is only ONE of the six. A river does not grow, does not feed, does not make young rivers.

A car is a good test case. It moves, and it even takes in fuel. But it does not grow, it cannot heal, and no car has ever produced a baby car. It fails most of the list, so it is not alive.

So do not use one sign. Check the whole list.
sections.example:
Sorting four things.

MANGO TREE
  Grows ✓  Feeds ✓  Breathes ✓  Makes seeds ✓
  → LIVING

RIVER
  Moves ✓  Grows ✗  Feeds ✗  Makes young ✗
  → NON-LIVING. Movement alone is not enough.

CHICKEN
  All six ✓
  → LIVING

WOODEN CHAIR
  Does nothing on the list now.
  → It is made from a tree that WAS alive, but the chair itself is not alive.

sections.heading: A tricky group
sections.body:
Some things were once part of a living thing but are not alive now: a wooden chair, a leather shoe, dried rice.

They came from something living. They are not living now. The test is always what the thing does TODAY — not where it came from.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Living or non-living? Give your reason using the list:

1. A cloud
2. A seed in the ground
3. A bicycle
4. Grass
5. A fire

Number 5 is worth thinking hard about. Fire moves, spreads and needs air — but does it grow the way a living thing grows? Does it make young?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Living things grow, feed, breathe, move, make young and respond.
• Check the WHOLE list, not one sign.
• Moving does not mean alive — rivers, cars and smoke all move.
• Something made from a living thing is not itself alive.

lessons.title: Parts of a Plant and What They Do

objectives.text: Name the main parts of a plant.
Say what job each part does.
Explain why a plant needs all its parts together.

keyTerms.definition: The parts under the ground that hold the plant and take in water.
The part that holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves.
The flat green part where the plant makes its food.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: A plant is not one lump. It is a set of parts, each doing a different job, and each needing the others.

sections.heading: The four main parts
sections.body:
ROOTS — under the ground.
  They hold the plant firm so wind does not blow it over,
  and they take in water from the soil.

STEM — the upright part.
  It holds the plant up towards the light,
  and carries water from the roots to the leaves.

LEAVES — the flat green parts.
  This is where the plant makes its own food, using sunlight.

FLOWER — where seeds are made.
  Seeds grow into new plants.

sections.heading: The parts need each other
sections.body:
Here is the important idea. No part can do its job alone.

The leaves make the food — but they cannot make it without water, and they cannot fetch water themselves.
The roots fetch the water — but they are underground in the dark and cannot make food.
The stem carries the water up — but it neither fetches nor makes anything.

So: roots fetch, stem carries, leaves make. Take away any one and the plant dies, even though the other two are unharmed.

This is why a cutting with no roots wilts, and why a plant kept in the dark dies even when it is watered every day.
sections.example:
Why a plant in a dark room dies.

You water it every morning. The soil is damp. Nothing is broken.

Roots — working. Taking in water ✓
Stem — working. Carrying water up ✓
Leaves — CANNOT WORK. They need sunlight to make food ✗

Two parts out of three are fine, and the plant still dies of hunger, standing in wet soil.

Water and food are not the same thing. This catches people out.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Which part takes in water from the soil?
2. Why would a plant fall over if its roots were cut?
3. A plant is in bright sun but has not been watered for a week. Which part cannot do its job, and why does that stop the leaves working too?
4. Name a plant part people eat. (Cassava, potato, spinach — which part is each one?)

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Roots hold the plant and take in water.
• The stem holds it up and carries water to the leaves.
• Leaves make food using sunlight.
• Flowers make seeds for new plants.
• Every part depends on the others — remove one and the plant dies.

questions.question: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.explanation: A mango tree grows, takes in water, breathes and makes seeds, so it does everything on the list. The others do none of it. A cloud changes shape and moves, but changing is not the same as growing.

questions.question: A river moves and never stops. Why is it still not a living thing?
options: Because it is made of water
Because it does not grow, feed or make young
questions.explanation: Moving is only one sign out of six. A river never grows, never feeds and never makes young rivers, so it fails almost the whole list. This is the mistake to avoid: check every sign, not just movement.

questions.question: Is a wooden chair a living thing?
options: Yes, because wood comes from a tree
No, because it does not do any of the things living things do
Yes, because it can last many years
questions.explanation: The chair came from a tree that WAS alive, but the chair itself does not grow, feed or breathe now. What matters is what the thing does today, not where it came from. Leather shoes and dried rice are the same — once part of something living, not living now.

questions.question: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.explanation: The roots are under the ground, where the water is. They also grip the soil so the plant does not fall over. The stem carries that water upward, but it does not collect it.

questions.question: Where does a plant make its food?
questions.explanation: The leaves make the food, using sunlight. Plants do not take food from the soil — they take WATER from the soil and make food themselves. Mixing up water and food is the most common mistake in this topic.

questions.question: A plant is watered every day but kept in a dark room. Why does it still die?
options: The leaves cannot make food without sunlight
questions.explanation: The roots and stem are working perfectly — water is coming in and going up. But leaves need sunlight to make food, and in the dark they cannot. The plant starves while standing in wet soil, because water and food are not the same thing.
